text: what little steadiness she had left. “You’re ok. Breathe.” His eyes tracked. Slowly. Found her face. The breath came in on the second try — ragged, effortful, dragging through him with an audible wheeze that she was going to think about later in her nightmares. His body trembled as it rebooted — spine arching slightly, hands twitching where they’d curled toward his chest. He rolled fully onto his back with a pained sound and stared up at the sky, lips parted, trying to remember what lungs were supposed to do. His limbs hurt terribly, his chest felt bruised from the inside. She stayed propped on her elbow beside him, watching his chest move, and felt something in her unclench that had been wound tight since she found her teammates washed up in the hall outside of the basement. He couldn’t form words yet. Might not for a while. His face was slack with fatigue, still trapped somewhere between fight and shutdown. But he was alive. He natural rules of the trial domains that kept the survivors running through hell were working out here. He would recover. They all would. And Orela — coughs still tearing through her lungs, dirt caked to her face, every limb screaming — laughed. She’d gotten him out. Behind them, the school looked... small. Not dramatically — it hadn't collapsed, hadn't crumbled, hadn't done anything as overt as announcing that it was finished. It had simply stopped. The Entity, spent and denied, had withdrawn Her influence, and without Her the building had exhaled back into itself — the swollen doorframes shrinking to ordinary gaps, the bloated wood settling, the geometry quietly returning to something that matched its original footprint. The rotten blockades were gone as if they'd never been there. The hallways that had doubled and tripled in the dark were just hallways again. The lights inside flickered gently, soft yellow through cracked panes. If it weren't for the playground, you might not have known. The yard told the story the building no longer would — mud churned deep by the flood, dark puddles catching the amber of the streetlamps, debris scattered across the asphalt. Planks and plaster. A locker half-buried in the fence. The ghost of a hopscotch grid somewhere under all of it, invisible now, possibly permanent. And six people. Sprawled and propped and collapsed in various arrangements across the mud — waterlogged, bleeding lightly from a collection of minor and not-so-minor insults, flinching from the streetlamp glow that had no business being this bright after hours of nothing. Broken. Shaking. Alive. All of them. Ch 12 – Remnant Someone found a medkit in a locked chest near the fence line. Nobody questioned it — the Fog providing in the particular way it sometimes did, not generously exactly, but adequately. Orela took charge of it, grateful for something she could actually do something about, and went through the group in order of need. Jake's leg first — the cut from the Entity's claw cleaned and wrapped properly, the makeshift bandana job finally retired. Dwight's collection of minor insults next, the desk-shaped bruise under his eye, the scrapes from the fence post, the general catalogue of having been bounced off several things at speed. Orela even found his glasses in a bush a short way from the fence, one lens cracked but both still in the frame, and watched something visibly settle in him when she put them back in his hands. David and Jake were still coughing. The wet, rattling kind that didn't shift, that sat deep and announced its intentions to stay for a while. The others hovered, which David tolerated with approximately the same grace he tolerated everything tonight — jaw set, waving hands away, accepting help only when it was faster than arguing about it. Somehow, he was still upright, though even he wasn’t sure how. Getting back to camp would likely see him sleep for days. Leon came back around slowly, blinking against the streetlamp glow and fighting back random waves of nausea when the world refused to settle. A few tries to get upright. A brief, undignified introduction to what dizziness felt like when it really committed. He sat with his back against the fence and let the world sort itself out, head against his knees and shaking hands hidden away against his torso. David slipped away from the group while Orela was occupied with Leon. He didn't go far — just far enough to breathe without someone checking on him, rolling his shoulder and cataloguing the damage. The wet rattle of his lungs had settled in for the long haul, and every time he thought it was clearing it came back with interest. He'd deal with it. Nothing lasts in the Fog anyways. Off to the farthest end of the yard, he could see Danny trying very purposely to keep to himself. The man had found a section of fence to lean against, away from the group, and was attempting to wrap his own ribs with a strip of some random strip of fabric he sourced for who knows where. The attempt was not going well. His hands were clumsy with it, the fabric not cooperating, and every time he tried to pull it tight, he flinched and lost his grip and had to start over. It was obvious that he either had never done it before, or more likely had been in the Fog for so long that he had forgotten how to tend injuries. Being untouchable for years on end would have that effect, David mused, watching him struggle with the task. It’d be funny if it wasn’t so pathetic. Something soft bounced off the side of Danny’s head, making him startle slightly. He mentally cursed himself for the reaction, nerves entirely wound too tight. Unlike this damned fabric.
